title: Piccoli A/S v. Calvin Klein Jeanswear Co.
lead: A Scandinavian distributor alleged discount imports destroyed its exclusive market; it could not enforce another licensee’s contract, but distinct unfair-competition and conspiracy claims survived the pleading motions.

actors.name: Calvin Klein Inc. (CKI)
actors.role: Beneficial trademark owner contracting with separate distributors

actors.name: Calvin Klein Jeanswear Company
actors.role: North American licensee accused of facilitating exports

actors.name: CK Jeanswear Europe, S.P.A. (European)
actors.role: European licensee later contracting with Piccoli

actors.name: Azteca and World Apparel
actors.role: Other alleged participants in the exporting scheme

actors.name: Judge Kaplan
actors.role: District judge deciding dismissal and judgment on pleadings

proceedings: Jeanswear and Azteca moved to dismiss and World Apparel sought judgment on the pleadings; court dismissed most theories while preserving Jeanswear Lanham Act and common-law unfair-competition claims and conspiracy allegations against the other two.
limits: Facts were allegations assumed on pleading motions, not findings of an export scheme or damages. The 1998 extraterritorial and notice-pleading analysis is historical. An anti-assignment clause alone was not held incompatible with third-party rights.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Separate distribution agreements divided the market
sections.cue: Introduce the contractual chain rather than treating every distributor as a party to one bargain.
paragraphs: In 1991, Calvin Klein Inc. (CKI), beneficial owner of the trademarks, gave Piccoli A/S exclusive Scandinavian distribution rights. Piccoli undertook minimum purchases, promotion, and sales through upscale retailers. It alleged investing marketing staff, thousands of hours, and hundreds of thousands of dollars in the market.

In 1994, CKI separately licensed Calvin Klein Jeanswear Company to manufacture, distribute, and wholesale in North America. Jeanswear could not sell outside that territory or to third parties it knew or should know would export beyond it. In May 1995, CKI licensed CK Jeanswear Europe, S.P.A., called European, for Europe. Piccoli’s direct CKI agreement expired in August, and Piccoli obtained Scandinavian exclusivity from European with essentially the same obligations. That apparent sublicense did not make Piccoli a party to Jeanswear’s contract.

sections.title: Piccoli alleged that discount imports displaced its customers
sections.cue: Follow the complaints, termination, and ensuing motions.
paragraphs: Piccoli alleged that from summer 1995 Jeanswear, Azteca, and World Apparel participated in shipping Jeanswear’s excess stock to Denmark for discount sale. Piccoli complained to European in February 1996. Upscale customers began complaining and canceling in March. CKI notified Jeanswear about Piccoli’s complaints before June 10, 1996.

European declined in October 1997 to join litigation against another Calvin Klein distributor. On December 18, Piccoli terminated its European agreement after learning European also exported into Scandinavia. Piccoli alleged continuing discount sales and loss of about ninety percent of its customers’ current and future business. Those were alleged market injuries, not adjudicated amounts.

Jeanswear and Azteca moved to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction and failure to state a claim; World Apparel sought judgment on the pleadings. Judge Kaplan assumed the complaint’s facts and considered incorporated contracts. No trial established the alleged scheme.

sections.title: The Jeanswear agreement preserved enforcement for its contracting parties
sections.cue: Apply both intended-beneficiary routes and the entire writing.
paragraphs: Under New York law, intended-beneficiary status could arise if nobody but the third party could recover for breach, or contractual language otherwise clearly authorized third-party enforcement. Piccoli failed the first route because CKI expressly retained damages and injunction remedies. European’s alleged opportunity to sue further weakened exclusivity. Piccoli’s motion-paper assertion of unique injury could not amend its pleading and, even considered, did not eliminate CKI’s enforcement right. Lost Piccoli purchases could injure European and ultimately CKI too.

Piccoli relied on Jeanswear’s promise to cooperate with CKI against diversion into other distributors’ territories. Naming Piccoli individually was unnecessary, but protective enforcement intent needed to appear on the face of the agreement. The court read cooperation with provisions making the agreement personal, restricting assignment and sublicensing without consent, and limiting binding effect and benefit to parties and permitted successors and assigns. Together they retained enforcement for those parties.

The court expressly rejected treating an anti-assignment clause alone as fatal to third-party rights; those concepts could coexist. Nor did Piccoli’s former direct-licensee listing necessarily cover its later sublicense status. Even assuming extrinsic circumstances were admissible, knowledge of the franchise, worldwide territorial cooperation, and investment did not overcome the text. Piccoli alleged an assumption that Jeanswear had parallel restrictions, not actual knowledge of its promise when signing with European. The contract count failed.

sections.title: Other labels did not supply the missing interparty undertaking
sections.cue: Explain the separately dismissed good-faith, restitution, and interference claims.
paragraphs: The implied covenant also failed because Piccoli had neither its own agreement with Jeanswear nor beneficiary rights under CKI’s agreement. The court declined a network-wide duty detached from a contract between these parties. Authorities recognizing tort duties arising from contracts did not establish one merely because firms held analogous distribution roles.

World Apparel proposed Danish law for nonfederal claims, but nobody identified an actual conflict, so the court applied New York law. Unjust enrichment required more than advantage from somebody else’s activity: Piccoli’s market-building work had to be rendered for defendants. It instead served Piccoli and perhaps customers, CKI, and European. Allegedly exploiting the resulting demand did not establish that quasi-contract obligation.

Because cancellations were not alleged to breach customer contracts, interference concerned prospective relations. Discount-channel sales were not directed at upscale customers to induce them to stop dealing with Piccoli. That indirect link failed the required direct-interference showing.

sections.title: Distinct marketplace duties allowed some claims to continue
sections.cue: Preserve the provisional nature of the federal territorial ruling.
paragraphs: Common-law unfair competition required a colorable property or financial interest, not necessarily trademark ownership. Piccoli’s exclusive distributorship supplied that interest when injury allegedly occurred despite later termination. Alleged bad-faith appropriation or passing off was not merely disguised contract enforcement: Piccoli lacked a contract with defendants, while market conduct supplied a potentially separate duty. The claim against Jeanswear survived.

The Lanham Act false-designation claim against Jeanswear also survived. Under the then-existing circuit framework for foreign conduct, the court examined substantial effects on United States commerce. The parties disputed domestic promotional materials, showroom negotiations, purchases, and shipments supporting foreign deception, and circuit cases varied on domestic activity’s significance. Alleged organized use of American commerce prevented exclusion of every possible basis on the pleadings; defendants could renew the issue on a fuller record. No required effect was conclusively found. Piccoli’s pecuniary interest supported its Section 43 theory although it lacked the ownership associated with Section 32 infringement.

The Paris Convention theory failed because controlling circuit law treated its Section 44 implementation as adding no substantive domestic rights. Azteca’s alleged manufacturing and shipping did not establish direct wrongdoing: it was not accused of obscuring address labels or knowingly violating an identified restriction. World Apparel’s proposed liability rested on conspiracy rather than direct acts.

sections.title: The pleaded coordinated scheme remained for further litigation
sections.cue: End with the precise defendant-by-defendant result.
paragraphs: The conspiracy allegations identified an agreement, overt acts, intentional participation, and harm sufficiently under New York law and the then-prevailing Rule 8 standard rather than Rule 9(b). For the federal claim, mere knowledge was insufficient, but knowing participation in a common scheme adequately alleged concerted conduct and control. That was pleading sufficiency, not a finding of agreement or involvement.

On September 8, 1998, Kaplan granted Jeanswear’s motion except for Lanham Act and common-law unfair-competition claims. He granted World Apparel’s judgment-on-the-pleadings motion and Azteca’s dismissal motion except for conspiracy allegations. No damages or final monetary remedy were awarded, and dismissal of the contract theory did not absolve every defendant of every claim.
